newsitem.title: UK: British women turn up heat on political parties.
newsitem.headline: British women turn up heat on political parties.

text.p: Women make up just over half of Britain's population but account for a relatively small number of seats in parliament and and figure even smaller when it comes to company directorships, an official said on Wednesday.
Women form 51 percent of Britain's population but less than 10 percent of its members of parliament and under three percent of company directors.
Inequality between the sexes is not new, but with Britain's general election at most eight months away, women are determined to flex their political muscles to do something about it.

"These are very shocking figures for Britain in the 1990s," Kamlesh Bahl, chairwoman of the Equal Opportunities Commission (EOC) of Great Britain, told a news conference. Women earn only 80 percent of men's average hourly pay and 4.6 million of them, compared to just 400,000 men, have independent incomes of less than 25 pounds ($39) a week.

The EOC has joined forces with the Women's National Commission (WNC), an official but independent body advising the government, to press Britain's main political parties to say where they stand on equality between men and women.

The two groups have prepared a detailed National Agenda for Action, consisting of 10 papers ranging from violence against women to access to the media, against which they will judge the parties' commitments.
"Our message to the politicians today is: you ignore this agenda at your peril," Bahl said.
She said that 82 percent of women eligible to vote at the last general election in 1992 did so, compared with an overall turnout of 77.8 percent.
"The voting pattern of women is the factor that will make a difference in the election of the next government. And the majority of floating voters are women," Bahl said.
Liz Bavidge, co-chairwoman of the WNC, said the political parties would be asked bluntly which parts of the women's agenda for action they were prepared to sign up to.
"Now is the time for ordinary women in this country to make their voices heard," she said.
One of the aims of the agenda is to ensure that the British government implements commitments it made at the World Conference for Women in Beijing last year.

Michael Trend, deputy chairman of the ruling Conservative Party, said the government had already acted in a number of areas raised by the agenda, including the provision of childcare places and increasing the number of women civil servants.

The opposition Labour Party's "shadow" minister for women, Janet Anderson, said her party's proposals for a minimum wage, and its steps to increase the number of women MPs, also helped meet the demands of the agenda for action. The minority Liberal Democrats likewise said their policies on women were very similar to those outlined by the two groups.

Bavidge, sounding sceptical, said: "We are encouraged that all three main parties have welcomed our agenda, but if they are serious about wanting to attract and hold on to women voters, they must do more than pay lip service to equality issues." ($1=.6428 Pound)
